sections.body:
A bathroom is the room where we wash ourselves. We use it to wash our hands, wash our face, brush our teeth and take a bath.

Every bathroom has the same big parts. There is a **sink**, where we wash our hands and face. There is a **mirror**, so we can see ourselves. There is a **toilet**, which some children call the loo. And there is a **bathtub** or a **shower**, where we wash our whole body.

There are also things that live on a shelf or in a cupboard. There is **soap** for washing hands. There is **shampoo** for washing hair. There is a **toothbrush** and **toothpaste** for teeth. There is a **towel** for drying. And there is a **comb** or a **hairbrush** for hair.

A bathroom is wetter than other rooms. Water goes on the floor, and water can make a floor slippery. So the bathroom is also the room where we must be careful.

When you know what each thing is for, the bathroom gets much easier. You can find what you need, and you can help your family keep it neat.
examples: This is my bathroom, where I wash myself.
I wash my hands at the sink.
The towel is on the hook.
sections.heading: What is a bathroom for?

sections.body:
Soap and water work together. Water washes the dirt away. Soap makes bubbles that carry the dirt with them. We put a little soap on wet hands and rub them together.

Shampoo is a special soap for hair. You put a little on your wet hair, then rub it gently. You do not scratch your scalp with your fingernails.

A **washcloth** or a small **sponge** is for the body. You dip it in the water, then rub your arms and legs.

A **toothbrush** has small bristles. You put **toothpaste** on the bristles, and you brush for about two minutes. You brush the fronts, the backs and the chewing sides of your teeth.

A **comb** has teeth. A **hairbrush** has longer bristles. You use them to brush your hair after you wash it, so the hair does not knot.

And a **towel** is a big soft cloth. You dry your body and your hair with it. A towel keeps you warm when you come out of the bath.
examples: I use soap on my hands.
The shampoo is for my hair.
I brush my teeth with the toothbrush.
sections.heading: The things we use to get clean

sections.body:
Hands touch everything. They carry germs from the ground, from the door handle and from other people. Washing them well keeps you and your family well.

Do these steps every time. It takes about twenty seconds, and it is worth it.

First, turn on the water and make it warm, not hot. Wet your hands and your wrists.

Then take some soap. Rub your palms together, then rub the backs of your hands.

Next, rub each finger. Slide your thumb around in your other palm, and rub between your fingers.

After that, rub your wrists and your nails. The germs hide there.

Finally, rinse well under the water and dry with the towel. Turn off the tap with the towel if you want to be extra clean.
examples: I wash my hands before I eat.
I rub between my fingers with the soap.
I dry my hands on the towel.
sections.heading: How to wash your hands the right way
steps: Make the water warm and wet your hands and wrists.
Take some soap and rub your palms together.
Rub the backs of the hands and between the fingers.
Rub your wrists and your nails.
Rinse well and dry with the towel.

sections.body:
These are the words for the things in a bathroom. Learn them, and you can ask for what you need.

A **sink** is the bowl where water comes out. You wash your hands and face in it.

A **tap** is the small handle or knob that turns the water on and off.

Soap is the slippery bar or liquid that makes bubbles in the water.

A **towel** is a soft cloth for drying your body and your hands.

A **toothbrush** is the small brush with bristles that cleans your teeth.

Say these words out loud as you walk around the bathroom. Point to each thing while you say it, and the words will stick.
examples: The sink is where I wash my face.

sections.body:
A bath is a nice warm treat. Some children have a bath every night. Others have one when they have been playing outside or when they feel dirty.

Before you get in, the floor can be slippery. Put down a **bath mat** so your feet have something to hold. An adult should check the water with their elbow first. The water should feel warm, never hot.

In the water you can play with **bath toys**. A rubber duck, a small boat or a cup for pouring water are all good toys. Pouring water from one cup to another teaches your hands to be careful.

When you finish, get out slowly. Hold the rail if there is one. Step onto the mat. Then dry yourself well, especially between your toes.

After a bath, your hair is wet and it can drip on the floor. A **towel** on your head helps. And a clean pyjama feels lovely after warm water.
examples: I put the rubber duck in the bath.
I step on the mat so I do not slip.
I dry my hair with a towel.
sections.heading: Bath time with bubbles and toys

sections.body:
The bathroom has water and hot things in it, so it needs care.

Wet floors are slippery. If the floor is wet, dry it at once. Say out loud, "The floor is wet."

Hot water can burn. Ask an adult to test the water before you get in.

Medicine is not a sweet. Pills and creams can look like sweets. Never take anything from the bathroom shelf. If you want something, ask an adult.

Sharp things belong to grown-ups. Razors, scissors and nail clippers go in a high drawer.

Never be alone near water. A bucket of water can be dangerous too. Children should not fill or empty buckets alone, and they should not play in the bathroom when it is busy.
examples: The floor is wet, so I wipe it now.
I ask an adult to check the water first.
I never touch the medicine box.
sections.heading: Staying safe in the bathroom

item.summary: The bathroom holds the things that keep us clean and well. After reading this, you can name the things in a bathroom, wash your hands the right way, and stay safe near water, hot water and sharp things.
item.title: Things We Use in the Bathroom
